title: Critical nonexplosion and phase transitions in finite-catalyst compartment systems
shortTitle: The exact boundary between fragmentation and explosion
oneLine: A complete phase diagram identifies when a finite-catalyst compartment population is conservative and when infinitely many events occur in finite time.
abstract: This research candidate classifies explosion for a stochastic population of noninteracting compartments with finitely many conserved catalysts, superlinear substrate production and content-dependent fragmentation. For production b+alpha(e)(s)_m and fragmentation kappa s^gamma, fragmentation prevents explosion when gamma>m-1 and, at the critical power gamma=m-1, exactly when alpha is at most kappa log(1/p). All other catalyst-containing finite states explode almost surely, whereas catalyst-free states remain conservative. The proof controls the complete descendant population rather than only an active lineage and proves the source conjecture. Extensions cover real exponents, logarithmic second-order boundaries, moment-controlled kernels and fresh random retained fractions Q, where the critical logarithmic loss becomes E[-log Q]. Equal mean retention need not determine the same phase. Explosive regimes also admit uniform exponential lifetime bounds at bounded catalyst count. Exact finite checks support selected algebra; the universal conclusions rest on the written proofs.

keyResults: For gamma>m-1 the process is conservative; for gamma<m-1 every finite catalyst-containing state explodes almost surely.
At gamma=m-1 the exact threshold is alpha <= kappa log(1/p), including equality.
With fresh random retention Q, the threshold uses E[-log Q] under one finite inverse moment and uniform conditional moment bounds.

narration: When can a mathematical population experience infinitely many events in finite time? In stochastic-process theory this is called explosion. It is a breakdown of the ordinary trajectory description, not a chemical detonation. This candidate studies compartments that contain substrate and a finite conserved number of catalysts. Substrate production accelerates as content grows, while fragmentation repeatedly splits a compartment and redistributes its contents. The paper identifies the exact phase boundary between these forces. If fragmentation grows faster than the critical power, the full population is conservative. If it grows more slowly, every finite state containing a catalyst explodes almost surely. At the critical power, the answer is decided by a sharp comparison between the production coefficient and the logarithmic loss at a split. The proof matters because following only one active lineage is not enough: discarded descendants can continue fragmenting and their events still count. The paper controls that passive population and then lifts the one-catalyst argument to any finite catalyst count. It also treats real growth exponents, a finer logarithmic boundary, general moment-controlled splitting and fresh random retention fractions. In that random setting the relevant quantity is the expected logarithmic loss, not the mean fraction retained; an explicit example shows that equal means can lead to different phases. Exact replay checks selected formulas in ordinary and optimized Python and deliberately corrupts inputs to verify rejection. Those checks support the calculations but do not prove the stochastic theorems. This is an unrefereed AI-assisted research candidate, not a formally verified result or external peer review. The paper, evidence and code are linked on the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

corrections.summary: Corrected three related-work links. Until 25 October 2026 this page and its machine record (paper.json) linked the source paper of Anderson, Howells and Rojas La Luz (2026) to arXiv:2601.11083, an unrelated paper; Brockwell, Gani and Resnick (1982) to doi:10.1017/S0021900200034622, which does not resolve; and Menshikov and Petritis (2014) to doi:10.1017/CBO9781107415324, an unrelated book. The correct references are *Bulletin of Mathematical Biology* 88, [doi:10.1007/s11538-026-01659-7](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11538-026-01659-7) (arXiv:2511.10223); *Advances in Applied Probability* 14(4), 709–731, [doi:10.2307/1427020](https://doi.org/10.2307/1427020); and *Stochastic Processes and their Applications* 124, 2388–2414, [doi:10.1016/j.spa.2014.03.001](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.spa.2014.03.001).
